# Writing standard

## Rules

- Lead with the answer or the decision in the first sentence, so a reader who stops after one line still knows what you need from them, what you decided, and by when it matters; put the reasons and the background after that, never before it.
- Write for someone who reads on a phone between meetings: short paragraphs of two or three sentences, one idea per paragraph, and a blank line between them, so the message can be skimmed quickly and nobody has to scroll back to find the question.
- When you disagree with someone, say what you agree with first, then say plainly what you see differently and why, using the facts both of you already have rather than opinions; offer one concrete next step that would settle it, and keep the tone calm even when the other message was sharp, because a reply written in a hurry is read slowly and kept for a long time by everyone on the thread.
- Say no clearly and early when the answer is no: name the request, give the real reason in one sentence, and, when you can, say what you could do instead and when; do not hide the refusal in the middle of a long paragraph or soften it until it reads like a maybe, because a vague answer costs the other person far more time and goodwill than a clear and kind refusal ever would.
- Use the words the other person used for their project, their product and their problem, even when your team calls it something else; it shows you read their message carefully and it keeps both sides from talking past each other in later replies.
- Prefer plain verbs to abstract nouns: write "we decided" rather than "a decision was made", and "please check" rather than "verification is requested"; plain verbs make it clear who does what, and they keep sentences short.
- Avoid stock phrases such as "I hope this finds you well" or "please do not hesitate to reach out"; start with the point and end when you are done.
- Put each question you need answered on its own line at the end, so the reader can answer them one by one without hunting through the text.
- Spell out acronyms the first time you use them with someone outside the team, and keep using the short form after that in the same thread.
- Match the formality of the person you write to: if they write casually, a casual reply is fine; if they write formally, stay formal until they change.
- Keep promises specific: say what you will do and when, and never promise a date that depends on someone else without saying so in the same sentence.
- Do not apologise more than once in a message, and never apologise for things that are not your fault just to sound friendly; one clear sorry is enough.
- Thank people for something specific they did rather than with a generic thanks at the end, so the thanks reads as meant and not as a habit.
- Reread the message once before it goes out, cutting every sentence that the reader would not miss, and check that names and figures are spelled correctly.
